questions.knowledge_point: Converting from Cartesian Coordinates to Polar Coordinates: Second or Third Quadrant
questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-8,-15).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$ Round your answer to two decimal places where necessary.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-8)^{2}+(-15)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64+225} \\  & =\sqrt{289} \\  & =17\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-15}{-8})| \\  & ≈1.080\,84.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the third quadrant, we add the reference angle to $\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +1.080\,84 \\  & ≈4.22,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places. Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(17,4.22).$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting from Cartesian Coordinates to Polar Coordinates for a Point on an Axis
questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(5,0).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies on the positive half of the $x$-axis, we have $\theta =0.$ 

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(5,0).$

questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(0,12).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{12}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{12}^{2}} \\  & =12\end{aligned}

Since the point $P$ lies on the positive half of $y$-axis, we have $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(12,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting from Cartesian Coordinates to Polar Coordinates: Second or Third Quadrant
questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-k,k),$ where $k$ is a positive real number. What are the polar coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-k)^{2}+{k}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{k}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-k}{k})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi $ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(\sqrt{2}\,k,\frac{3\pi }{4}).$

questions.problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-\sqrt{3},1).$ Find the polar coordinates of $P.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{-\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi $ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(2,\frac{5\pi }{6}).$
